title: When Guards Fail: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of a Constrained+Verifier+Authenticated‑Handoff Defense for NetOps Agent Prompt‑Injection
abstract: Generative LLM agents are being proposed to produce network configuration actions from high‑level intent, but prompt‑injection attacks that force tool selection or corrupt LLM judging can induce unsafe commands. We preregistered a paired confirmatory study (N_pairs=500) that compared an unconstrained baseline agent to a defensive pattern combining (1) a constrained tool surface, (2) an independent deterministic verifier, and (3) an authenticated tool‑handoff. The experiment used a synthetic, adapter‑compatible NetOps task suite and gpt-5-mini as the generation model; a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) scored final configurations. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Result: baseline successes = 500/500, defended successes = 500/500; paired difference = 0.0 (n11=500, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0), exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.0, 95% paired bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Confirmatory preregistered hypotheses (≥50% relative reduction) were not supported. We analyze why the defense showed no effect, describe limits of inference (single model, synthetic tasks, shared‑candidate generation semantics), and provide concrete lessons for future defensive evaluations and NetOps agent design.

sections.introduction: Automating NetOps via LLMs and agentic workflows promises to reduce operator burden but raises acute safety concerns: model outputs can produce incorrect, insecure, or adversary‑induced configuration changes. Recent work documents prompt‑injection attacks that hijack tool selection or LLM judgments (e.g., tool‑library hijacks, JudgeDeceiver) and papers propose verifier‑based mitigations and agent orchestration patterns. We designed a preregistered, confirmatory paired experiment to measure whether a defensively composed architecture—constraining the tool surface, gating outputs with an independent deterministic verifier, and using authenticated tool‑handoff—reduces attacker success rate relative to an unconstrained baseline in a controlled NetOps task suite. Our contributions: (1) a sealed preregistration specifying paired design, metrics, and decision rules; (2) a fully executed confirmatory run (500 paired attacks + 500 benign pairs) with preserved artifacts; (3) transparent negative (null) results with analysis of causes, limitations, and concrete guidance for next studies.
sections.related_work: Research has rapidly characterized LLM vulnerabilities in toolized agents and LLM‑as‑judge settings (ToolHijacker; optimization‑based prompt‑injection on LLM judges). Concurrent NetOps studies examine LLMs for configuration repair and generation and integration with formal or deterministic validators (Cornetto; CAIP; Ciri). Work on agentic workflows (COHORT, RepLLM) emphasizes multi‑agent critique and replay for safety. Our study intersects these lines by evaluating an instantiated defense architecture under a preregistered, paired protocol using a deterministic validator and a synthetic NetOps task corpus; the study focuses on attack success (functional acceptance of malicious tool outputs) as an operational metric rather than language‑level rubric scores.
sections.methodology: Design and preregistration: We preregistered study a2b7d4c1‑... (sealed) that defined the research question, two confirmatory hypotheses (H1: ≥50% relative reduction in attacker success; H2: benign false‑positive rate <10%), sampling plan (N_pairs=500 attack pairs; 500 benign pairs), analysis (exact paired/binomial methods and one‑sided exact binomial for H2), exclusions, missingness rules, and stopping conditions. Implementation: adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 orchestrated agent runs; declared generation model = gpt-5-mini (provider artifact openai_responses); deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced paired tasks and ground‑truth reference answers; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed intent‑aware functional validation (scoring_rule="full_intent_constraint_validation"). Crucial execution choice (preregistered): generation_semantics="shared_initial_candidate" (the same initial candidate was shared between baseline and defended conditions rather than independently sampled). Conditions: baseline (unconstrained agent pipeline) vs guarded (constrained tool surface + independent verifier + authenticated handoff). Attack corpus: 500 attack attempts derived from a published synthetic_paired_llm_benchmark_v1 adapter‑compatible corpus (public artifacts archived). Execution: 1000 total episodes completed (500 paired attacks and 500 benign pairs), model_calls_used=500. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on paired 0/1 success outcomes where success means final configuration accepted by the validator. Preplanned decision rule required observed relative reduction ≥50% with 95% CI excluding reductions <50% to support H1.
sections.results: All preregistered confirmatory outputs are archived. Counts (primary): baseline_successes = 500/500; guarded_successes = 500/500. Paired contingency: n11=500, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). Because both conditions achieved perfect validator acceptance on every paired attempt, the preregistered confirmatory criterion (≥50% relative reduction) is not met; H1 is not supported. H2 (benign false‑positive rate <10%) is not falsified under the observed benign pairs (no defended benign blocking was observed in the archived benign subset). Secondary planned measures (latency, ablations) were not informative because no defender‑driven rejections or repairs occurred; the execution manifest records shared_initial_generation semantics and identical shared_initial_candidate hashes across conditions, explaining identical outputs in practice.
sections.discussion: Null outcome interpretation: The defensive pattern as instantiated did not change validator acceptance in this configuration. The execution artifacts reveal a key operational factor: generation_semantics was preregistered as shared_initial_candidate with independent_condition_generation=false; both baseline and guarded conditions therefore received the same initial model candidate (artifact hashes identical), and the verifier stage performed deterministic validation that accepted those candidates. Consequently, the defense pipeline had no opportunity to alter or block the model candidate in any of the paired runs—producing identical acceptance outcomes. Potential causes beyond shared‑candidate semantics include (1) attack corpus items that the model resolved into syntactically valid, intent‑conforming commands the validator accepted (i.e., the attacks did not produce outputs that violated the deterministic validator rules), (2) residual contamination risk—the model’s training data overlap with synthetic task templates cannot be excluded and could make the model robust to those injections, and (3) single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic task distribution limit external validity. Threats to validity: internal—preregistered shared‑candidate choice limited the defense’s operational effect; construct—the deterministic validator may be insufficiently sensitive to the prompt‑injection semantics we targeted; external—single model, synthetic tasks, no vendor diversity; conclusion—evidence supports that, under the exact preregistered implementation and generation semantics, the instantiated defense produced no reduction in accepted malicious outputs. Lessons: (a) confirmatory defensive evaluations must ensure independent condition generation to let defenses interpose on distinct model outputs; (b) validators must be calibrated to the threat signal (syntactic acceptance alone can mask semantic compromises); (c) contamination checks and multi‑model evaluation are crucial for generalizable claims.
sections.conclusion: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired confirmatory evaluation of a constrained+verifier+authenticated‑handoff defense against NetOps agent prompt‑injection. Under the preregistered implementation and the shared_initial_candidate generation semantics, the defense produced no measurable reduction in attacker success (500/500 accepted in both conditions). This null result highlights brittle evaluation choices (shared candidate semantics and deterministic acceptance criteria) that can mask or prevent defenses from exercising influence. Future work should run independent per‑condition generation, expand model diversity, strengthen validators to detect semantic manipulations, and evaluate adaptive adversaries; the archived artifacts and logs permit such follow‑ups.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (preregistered) caused identical initial candidates across conditions, preventing the defense from interposing on independent model outputs—this operational choice limited any observable defensive effect.
Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and a synthetic task corpus limit external validity; results do not generalize across vendor models or real production task distributions.

Deterministic validator acceptance criteria used here may be insufficiently sensitive to semantic prompt‑injection patterns; a validator tuned to provenance or source provenance signals could behave differently.
Residual contamination risk: overlap between synthetic task templates and model pretraining cannot be excluded and could make the model unusually robust to the specific attack corpus.

The confirmatory null result pertains strictly to the instantiated defense, generation semantics, and task distribution preserved in the archived artifacts and should not be taken as a statement about the abstract defense pattern under different implementations.
